review_text: Max is an INCREDIBLY lazy professor. It truly feels like he puts in 0 time to preparing for lectures because his slides are often incomplete or a mess, he doesn't know the answers to any questions students ask during class (or he gives the vaguest hand-wavy response), and he frequently ends lecture 30 minutes early because he's run out of things to say. It feels like he himself doesn't fully understand what he's teaching sometimes. Like the other reviews note, he also fills a bunch of lecture time with unrelated thoughts and work stories, and while the class seems to find them entertaining (and Max loves the attention and reactions he gets from saying all his unpopular or taboo things), it would be better if there was more real content time to match. Max doesn't believe in studying any of the data science concepts rigorously, and while teaching a survey of topics at a high-level could be acceptable, he doesn't even touch on enough topics to make the class worthwhile. Instead, we learn in an entire semester basically what someone could get from reading a few articles on data science for a few hours. He also assigned multiple hours worth of youtube videos this semester in lieu of teaching the topics himself, and made the content directly testable on the exams. His reading-based exam questions (which constitute a significant portion of each exam grade) are genuinely trivia and not relevant to any fundamental understanding of data science concepts. He isn't active in responding to people's concerns on Piazza, mistakes are abundant in his posted materials, and policies seem to change frequently (such as him announcing a flat 11% curve on exam 1 then never following through on it). Overall I find it difficult to give a higher rating to a professor who transferred such little knowledge to his students and put in such little effort into his full-time teaching job. I excelled in this class (and you definitely can too) by always going to lecture, reviewing the slides carefully before exams, memorizing major points from the readings, and thinking critically about what Max must be looking for while answering exam questions.

Cliff and Anwar typically are the only people who teach this. Material is the same but definitely take Anwar over Cliff. Cliff's lectures are about as boring as can be. Imagine a theatre kid mixed with a introverted CS nerd. I would have rather watched paint dry than attend another one of his lectures as it would've been more entertaining and helpful than his lectures. His notes and slides are a mess filled with snazzy little transitions that make it a nightmare to navigate. The class overall felt pretty unstructured with random topics thrown in for the s and g's. At least Anwar recorded his lectures and explained things better than Cliff's philosophical mumbling. Material is difficult but certainly doable. Start project 5 early. TA's were hit or miss. I think there were maybe one or two good ones but the rest seemed to be pretty rude, unhelpful, or overall useless. My discussion TA was late half the time and spent most of the time arguing with one student about different ways to do problems. That's all I remember until I stopped showing up to the discussion at all.

Nelson is knowledgeable and teaches the material decently but he is unprofessional. He often distracts from the material and embarrasses students, like calling out a student for her insulin pump beeping. He shouldn't have to make jokes at the expense of a student to engage his class because not every student is comfortable being put on blast in front of the whole class. This behavior discourages students from coming to class and creates an uncomfortable environment for those that he picks on and students that have to watch. He does grade fairly and records lectures which is nice. He seems to care about students a lot but continues to act rudely towards them.

I don't really see the hype. Don't get me wrong, he is good, but so is Fawzi. On pure lecturing, Fawzi is actually better, but overall interaction with students in office hours and stuff like that, I'll give that to Justin. There are a couple of other Lecturers too. The hype for Justin is RIDICULOUS, lol. The class is heavily weighted on Exams. You make a small mistake, you lose a lot of points -> you get a bad grade in the class. That's not Justin's fault, I guess, since the class is a theory course. Justin made A LOT of errors on the midterms. How's that for the GOAT teacher, huh? What a joke. Oh I almost forgot, lectures being 8 AM, I wish he recorded the lectures. Well, bro wakes up at 4 AM everyday so. Just take Ting.

One of the best professors I have had at UMD. As other reviewers mentioned, she is very responsive on Piazza. She is also very lenient with the deadlines. Her exams and projects are fair and as long as you study her slides you will be fine. She genuinely wants her students to do well and I am glad that I took this course with her. Would 100% recommend her!

This is one of those courses where the lecture has nothing to do with the project. The professor is decent lecturing about operating systems concepts, but you're stuck with the TAs to get you through the project which is probably the hardest project in your entire college career.

Goat lecturer but just be aware his grading takes FOREVER. Like at least a month for exams and projects and like a week for final. We didn't get back 2 project grades (worth 30% of our grades) until 5 days after the final. He does give a good amount of extra credit points for projects so be sure to take advantage of that. Exams are all pretty fair, the first two projects were pretty easy but the last two took a good amount of time (Try to start early). His research is so cool, don't skip his classes cuz they are so interesting. He also records so thats another plus.

Everyone here is complaining for no reason, i'm taking this class right now and the exams and projects are challenging but not to the point that some of these reviews are saying. I've learned so much through this course and can actually retain information because of his teaching and exam structures. The exams are basically the exact same as the practice problems and one night of studying before the exam will literally get you at least an 80%. He also pushed back project deadlines SOO often if anyone asked. I'm by no means coasting through this class and I am not a particularly bright student but I enjoyed this class and would take it again despite the 7 exams.

loved taking cmsc421 with Pratap. him teaching it definitely made it the favorite upper level cs class that i've taken at umd. slide decks are structured very well and provide a ton of information, all of which i found really interesting. homeworks and projects are very interesting to work on and he provides practice exams for his exams, so you know what to expect on exams and can prepare really well for them. 10/10 experience for me and would highly recommend taking cmsc421 with Pratap to anybody.

nothing good to say. All the reviews from this year pretty much echo how I feel. I hope Marine Carpuat reads over these reviews and considers modifying the syllabus/course structure for the students taking this next year.

this class was absolutely atrocious. the participation quizzes were not in fact graded on participation/completion, but rather on accuracy. the weekly readings are tedious and dense, and the reading quizzes themselves are a monstrosity. all of the projects are taken from another university, so the codebase is super deep and complex. there is very little guidance on implementing the required methods, and the difficulty of the projects do not match the information learned from the reading quizzes. onto the next: exams. the most vile questions are cooked up to test every single edge case of our knowledge. algorithms are confusingly modified to test if we have a master's level of understanding of databases, and the questions are specifically tailored to trip us up. the other reviews below can confirm this, abadi seems to find great joy in this. cool class and important concepts, but i did not anticipate this class to be the hardest class i have ever taken at my university. truly tragic when trying to load balance your schedule and this abomination of a class appears out of nowhere.

This course is literally the continuation to CMSC330 but more. Uses functional language (but in Racket not Ocaml) to develop compiler and interpreter. Professor is a very smart, enthusiastic, and kind professor. Notes are posted online and the lectures are recorded, which is very helpful for review. Projects can be tedious but are manageable if you dont procrastinate. Exams are TAKE HOME and 24-hour! This is very different but I liked it tbh. Note: the 1st exam is easy but the 2nd is much more difficult. I spent like a straight 12 hours working on it to pass all cases. They say that you should be able to finish in a normal class period but that's not even remotely true if you want a good grade lol.

Genuinely one of the worst structured classes I have ever taken. It felt like they threw the course together without any forethought. The course grades consisted entirely of projects and one midterm which occurred during the first quarter of classes. For a course whose material was centered around projects, the projects themselves felt random, and disorganized, and had a zero-tolerance policy for late submissions. Anything submitted after 11:59 on the due date would result in an instant 0% on the assignment. This has been one of the most stressful experiences of my college career.

For clarity, I'll quickly explain the class format. 5 assignments that are worth 40% of your grade with the lowest score being dropped, one midterm (that is awkwardly placed at about a third of the way through the semester) that is worth 20% of your grade, and a final that is "cumulative" and worth another 40%. There is also a hefty curve in the class which can be upwards of 6-7% some years -- typically depends on the difficulty of the exams that year. Regarding the assignments, they are pretty challenging. They often can take between 10-20 hours (especially dynamic programming one) and lots of work since each problem involves understanding all the underlying concepts, inventing/creating an algorithm, proving it works with some reasonable degree of certainty (instructors tend to be lenient about how "good" your proof is if you're right though), and proving it works in the runtime bound. Definitely start early, and definitely make frequent visits to office hours to bother the TA's and ask them to review through your work since ultimately they are the ones grading the assignments. Regarding the midterm, it was weirdly placed. The midterm was placed at the same time classes that typically have 2 midterms have their fist midterm (around end of first week beginning of second week of October). Otherwise, that midterm was relatively straightforward conent-wise -- those who didn't do well either couldn't brainstorm the gimmick to answer the question on the exam, or simply didn't review and study enough. The average on that exam was about a 68%. The final, in my opinion, was slightly harder. It covers a significantly higher breadth of topics than the midterm. In my opinion, the depth that each question goes into in the topic was a bit lower since most of the questions were very similar to questions on previous practices or other CMSC451 finals practices you could find online. The final on its own isn't that challenging, however, with much of the content being straightforward from the textbook. So long as you practice the standard questions, you really should be fine. The best part of Child's class is lectures. His lectures are just amazing. They are well put-together, easy to follow, and also have just enough "question the class to see what the class is thinking" but enough "let's guide through the class so we get some sh*t done". Laxman (the other well renowned and highly rated CMSC451 teacher who also taught Fall 2024) came and gave in a guest lecture, and I was absolutely surprised in the difference in quality between the lectures. Although Laxman's lecture wasn't "bad", it just really pointed out to me how much Child's lectures have an almost 3blue1brown feel because of how nice they flow. Some other misc things: he's pretty active on Piazza so that's really nice. Some of the TA's don't know a lot about these problems (and that follows because a lot of them naturally don't work in this field and might have other preoccupations), so they might also get stuck or not be able to help out on problems so try and exhaust all the TA's office hours and Child's office hours when stuck on homework. Child's expertise is in quantum algorithms so if you need anything with that or are interested, definitely feel free to talk to him about it. He tries to spend a lecture covering basic quantum algorithms at the end of the course but sometimes he doesn't have time to do that (like this semester), but regardless, you should look into it if interested. Overall, I had a lot of fun in this course and it's a definite recommend (even over other CMSC451 sections -- including Laxman's). While you might not necessarily get much practical implementation value out of the course, it's a lot of fun, and definitely molds your brain to become better and more versed in the world of reading and understanding algorithmic problems (which can be infinitely valuable when doing things like Leetcode or software interviews). If you have any math background or are interested in any algorithms stuff, definitely take the course!

Never take his class. Wait it out till another Professor teaches 470. He is very arrogant and looks down at UMD students, flaunting his Ivy League background. I mean sure, but why crush the confidence of students like you are literally a faculty at the same place you look down upon? He is also very image conscious and will make sure that he does not have to take critical decisions while showing no empathy for students during the COVID-19 waves. He does not give class lectures and there are videos already up on his class, so what is the point of attending the class? His coding assignments were weird with no semblance to latest ML and NLP industry practices. Also he teaches a very obsolete part of Q&A like yeah okay, then rename the course as Q&A not NLP. He has this weird obsession about trivia competitions like not every person in NLP has to do trivia. His class was one of the absolute worst at UMD.

I didn't learn much from Cruz. The two quizzes, while not worth much of your overall grade, each had an average of about 55%. Everything else I want to say has already been said in other reviews. All in all, don't take this professor!

I feel upset because Professor Duffy is overall a kind person and not a horrible teacher. However, that being said, it felt like she was really unresponsive to elms messages (her preferred communication) and had poor communication with not only her students but her TAs as well. I was thankful to have a wonderful discussion TA to help me during this class. As someone said too, there was a big academic dishonesty case in the class, and I was a part of it simply for being in the group chat. I do not blame her for what had happened, but I do feel a little bitter over the fact I begged for help and had such bad communication to resolve the matter. Other than that, I did enjoy the textbook and think it is an easy read for the class. PLEASE pick people who have good work ethics for the group project, I am very thankful I had such kind and hardworking teammates, it makes the class way more enjoyable.

At the moment this professor seems genuinely seems busy with all the things going on in his life. Which is fine but that comes at a cost to his courses. This course is likely terrific if you already know all of the concepts and ideas that he asks for in assignments and exams. However, if you remotely struggle in this course there are very few resources available to you and it's extremely difficult to get in contact with the professor. Even when you do you frequently have to follow up in order to get any form of help. This problem is only made worse since this semester the TA while being a great person didn't give a lot of help in the sometimes vague questions or when you were genuinely stuck. This professor is best suited for students who require minimal help to understand data science and can quickly finish assignments since due dates aren't consistent.

MATH140– Literally the worst, nice person but awful teacher. Class avg for the first exam was a 30, and from there on was around a 60, which is not good. Multiple times in class, she essentially called us stupid for not being able to opt out of the class due to not getting the AP credit etc. She would also single out kids who asked questions, and would answer their questions with a response that was formulated to make them feel stupid. Class was around 150 students, and after the first 2 weeks, around 20 kids showed up consistently to class, since her teaching was a joke. If you can, DO NOT TAKE HER.

Amazing professor. My class was the first he taught as a professor rather than as a TA, and he is genuinely one of the best math professors out there. His lectures are extremely well-organized, and he consistently encourages students to ask questions. Although I never personally attended his office hours, many classmates shared that he patiently works through problems with you step by step and makes sure you truly understand the material. We had weekly quizzes, usually consisting of one or two questions taken directly from the worksheets he posted on ELMS before each quiz, which made them very fair. He also provided practice exams that closely mirrored the actual midterms. Overall, he is a great professor, and it’s clear he wants every single student to succeed.

Professor Wong is an elite professor. You learn so much from him and he clearly is like one of the most knowledgeable people you'll ever meet when it comes to math. His lectures are fast-paces but it doesn't really feel rushed or that you aren't up to speed with the material. I also think he covers some extra topics (not on the final) at the end of the semester to talk about the important of Linear Algebra which I found was quite interesting and unique, showing just how much he cares about students understanding why they are taking the course and their practical applications in the real world. There are weekly quizzes, but they are the easiest quizzes you'll ever take. He essentially tells you exactly what is going to be on the quiz, and the TAs cover those topics before you take the quiz. For me, I pretty much never studied for them because they were so easy and straightforward. Discussion was extremely valuable. the TAs are really smart and explain things in a phenomenal manner. If you have any questions about literally anything, you can just ask them and they will help you out. As for exams, Professor Wong is very clear is what is going to be covered. There are never any trick questions, but the exam is very theory heavy. Be sure to understand what you're actually doing because there are a lot of T/F questions and others that test your actual understanding, not merely following a pattern to compute things. He also provides practice exams and they are pretty similar for what you would expect for the exams. I didn't really have to study much for the exams because it was all very straightforward and Professor Wong and the TAs really give you everything you need to success. I would say the final was definitely harder than the midterms (which is expected), so definitely study hard for it. But very reasonable and follows a similar structure and pattern to previous exams which are all given. Overall, I couldn't recommend a better professor for 240. As a CS major, you actively learn some of the applications of Linear Algebra and learn a lot from Professor Wong.

I watched my degree evaporate before my eyes on the final. Please don't take this man if your life depends on it. His exams were nothing like the HW, quizzes, or practice exams he gave us. He told us point estimators were not going to be a major topic of the final since we only learned it for a week, but then proceeded to make it 25% of the final exam, which is worth 40% of your grade. Pincus is a nice dude though and will answer all your questions. He also only reads off the slides and his lectures aren't more helpful than looking through a textbook

bros the goat, easy class. easy A. thank god I took him. if he keeps this up, he's the obvious choice for 401. it's a basic requirement anyway, so the shortfalls of his class don't really matter. take Anurag, keep your sanity.

Overall, Pedram is a solid professor. He explains concepts clearly ( even if boring) , is approachable, and makes the class manageable. He records his lectures, gives a short mid-lecture break, and provides detailed exam and quiz outlines, which were especially helpful when studying. Where he tends to fall short is in exam alignment. The material taught in lecture and shown on practice exams is often much easier than what appears on the actual exams. As a result, the real exams feel significantly harder and less representative of what we are given. This is reflected in the exam averages, which were around a C surprisingly low for an introductory CS course where many students already have prior coding experience. Because of this, I would not recommend this class with Pedram as a first exposure to coding. However, for students who already have programming experience and can handle higher-difficulty exam questions, he is a reasonable choice and overall a decent professor.

I took Elias for 131 and 132 and I will say that he is definitely the best introductory CS professor anyone could ask for. I was very scared coming into UMD because I had pretty much no true coding experience (I had not even taken AP CS principles) and I had heard from various planetterp reviews and forums that this course would be difficult if I did not already have at least some background in CS. However, Elias made both of these courses a great experience. He truly cares about his students and takes time to talk about topics such as mental health. He also has a system set up so that there are nearly constant office hours making it very easy to get help with projects or leading up to exams. His lectures were also very engaging. He explained concepts very well (especially for someone with no prior knowledge) and was always very receptive to questions (as I used to ask a lot especially in 132), making sure his answers contained as much depth as possible. In addition to being a great teacher and having a system that makes it easy to get help, he also records lectures, provides a plethora of practice material for midterms and the final, and overall is just a very approachable person. Would definitely recommend.

Really well ran course. The projects were pretty instructive, especially the Assembly project. Considering that the tests are borderline open internet, they're surprisingly easy, and if you can do the projects, you can definitely do well on the exams. There's so many places to get bonus points, so even if you lose some points here or there, you can get them back really easily. The lectures can be a bit slow at times, but physical attendance isn't mandatory so if that's an issue you can just watch the lecture videos at your own pace. He loves answering questions, so if you're struggling with a concept, he'll make sure you understand it. Taking 216 with Kauffman really is a no-brainer, just do it.

40% hw grade + 10% discussion grade so u essentially cannot fail, and pretty good lecturer when hes not realizing that his slides are completely wrong lmao. idk if this is good or bad but u can get by comfortably with almost never studying

It's hard to review him because there is so much good and bad about him. If you go to lectures, he'll explain stuff really well and he's super considerate and nice, but there'll be just random moments where its like hes looking at his own slides for the first time in years. That was kinda annoying, but its eh. The homeworks are super easy, I think the median for all of them was 100. They feel like easy points, and the instructions are super vague, so it kind of lets you have room to do whatever, as long as its clear you took something away from it. I thought they were way better the coding assignments you would get in like 330 where its just follow the instructions and code it. As for the exams, he makes a point about how theyre supposed to test your understanding of the material rather than how well you memorized it, but I honestly didn't feel that. Just study for the first exam to get a feel for what the questions are like, because his exam writing style is very unique

TLDR, if you have a choice between Anwar of Cliff, take Anwar (better overall lectures and more do able assessments). Cliff personally made this course much harder than it was supposed to be. I usually ended up reading Anwar's slides and examples, and eventually, watch his recordings instead to understand some weird concepts like lambda calculus. Cliff notes made it insanely harder to understand and grasp it in my opinion. The way he designed his slides is just so not intuitive at all, and makes it even harder when he doesn't record his lessons. He has philosopher style of teaching, which makes sense because he got a degree in that. But honestly, teaching cs in that kind of style just makes it harder and more complicated than it's supposed to be for students to understand this class. And remember, 330 is a required class as a cs major, so yeah this matter should be taken seriously rather than a joke. Now yes, keep in mind, 330 is a hard class (it's a 300 level course duh). So yeah regardless it wasn't going to be an easy class anyway. But I just felt like this course was insanely unstructured. They taught things too fast and concepts just felt out of place to grasp personally, especially when it's expected that many students are also taking this class with 351. I also felt like the projects were way too complicated and just weren't helpful in understanding the concepts that we learned in the course, especially project 5. And I also think we could've just learned Rust for the entire course rather than jumping into a new language after already a difficult language (OCaml) weeks before our final. Also, I despised the fact that the course used OCaml to teach us the concepts, honestly made things worse to click and understand... I just felt like if they assessed things with more structure, and actually know what kind of questions to ask on the exams, the course wouldn't have been to hard. Because honestly, the concepts were actually darn easy to grasp, and some of them were pretty cool and essential too (e.g. NFAs/DFAs).

Since I already had experience with web programming, this was one of the easiest CS classes I've ever taken. Nelson doesn't require attendance, so I showed up only for the midterms. He provides many resources to use when studying so you're never unprepared. One neat thing about the final project is it's up to you to design and implement it.
If she is co-teaching with Justin again -- 5/5. Her exams are more fair, and she is a very nice person and a lenient grader. Just study off of Justin's notes and do well on the midterms

Big up professor Asgari. The content she teaches in her architecture class are REALLY interesting, and the projects are so fun and educational. You really get a lot out of this class - she's super active on Piazza and is so helpful with clarifications. She's very accommodating of students' needs and requests, and you can tell she's a very genuinely nice person and wants her students to succeed. I loved this class - it's my favorite 400 level CS class so far, and it's definitely thanks in part to her projects and kindness. My one issue would be that her lectures are somewhat dry; while the content is super interesting, when lecturing she doesn't do much more than read from the slides monotonically and answer questions. The exams are fair and she's always open to help with students' questions.

As other students have and will continue to write, I would give this a 0. As others have noted, 412 is a useful skill, so one should take it? No. It is one of my biggest regrets at UMD. There are literally 20 reasons to not take this course, but some of them include: Asking a question about a project that was not due until a week after the exam, which was weighted 18% of the exam grade; Having TA's not reply to almost all piazza posts, and never replying the 4-5 days leading up to a project due date; Giving "Routine" pop quizzes (there were 2); Having a Participation grade (Went to every class except 1 -- had a pop quiz on that class, and I got an 80 on participation (12 points lower than average)); Having a 52% on the final exam; The professor not even making his own slides, rather uses the slides that the textbook gives; has both slides and a spec for projects, both with information relevant, but only found on one or other; Hiding the final not on gradescope where all previous exams and quizzes were placed. There are literally so many more reasons, but just trust me don't take the class with this guy. He comes off as nice, but he grills students for coming in late, but half the class doesn't even show. I could guarantee he doesn't even know the questions on the exam also. Just avoid.

wonderful lecturer and really cool guy! it's a hard class but he's super passionate about the material and it shows in every class, so the course was really enjoyable despite the difficulty and i feel like i learned a lot projects and exams were really challenging and grades take a while to get back, but tas and class materials were pretty helpful with both of them

After reading all of these opinions on the 7 exam structure, I wanted to join and say I actually really enjoyed it. This was one of my favorite CS classes ever. Instead of cramming for large exams with a bunch of different concepts, I was able to focus on just two at a time and actually learn! The exams line up very well with the practice problems and are not very difficult. The number of exams and the fact that Justin drops some is also very forgiving if you have an off week. Overall, Justin is an amazing lecturer and the structure of this class was very fair in my opinion. I learned a lot.
I had him for 320 got an A. This dude is lowkey buns. Imagine a professor who wants to teach but is lazy ash. That's basically him. He's just a troll. Why did I have to have him again for 421.

I have never actually had such a bad professor that makes me want to write a review for them here. Her slides are extremely vague and barely help. You are expected to memorize so many things even when she doesn't explicitly state it, and the practice problems are practically useless considering that the exam will be some theoretical concept she mentioned maybe once. It also seems like this class is at the bottom of her priorities and as if she needs half the class to fail in order to enforce high standards. I would advise you save your mental sanity and take this course with someone else as you'll put in hours on end to still end up lost during lectures and exams.

Very well-structured course where you are told exactly what is expected of you. He follows the textbook very closely and has detailed online slides. His grading is pretty good, sometimes a bit strict. Projects were relatively easy. Practice exams and homeworks were close to the actual exams. Second time taking this prof and would take a course by him again.

This has been one of the more interesting classes I've taken at UMD. It's very structured because the course format has stayed the same for many years (since Calderon taught it), but not much of that can be attributed to DVH himself if im being honest. The lectures were super useless, all they really involved were DVH going through tangential Racket code in his Racket REPL. Half the time, we would barely get through any of the topics in the lecture notes. That being said, the projects were really interesting for this class and the course notes are super helpful. A lot of these were created by Professor Calderon I think and they are super useful, and what made the class really rewarding in the end. If you take this class with DVH, I highly recommend checking out Jose's online videos / notes. They honestly were WAY more useful than going to DVH's lectures in my opinion. My experience with the TAs was definitely hit or miss. Some of the TAs were very sweet, caring, and helpful. We had really good response times on Piazza (shoutout Pierce!!), and some of the OH TAs were great and really caring. That being said, some of the TAs just felt underprepared and careless about the class. Sometimes, I felt that they didn't really know much about the projects or how to implement them, which made office hours unproductive for me on several occasions. The midterms were alright and felt very fair. DVH definitely does a good job making these, and gives very fair review materials and practice midterms. There are a handful of quizzes and surveys throughout the semester, but be careful not to miss them. I remember them being about 15% of our grade, and if you're even a little bit late, you get a 0 no exceptions. Overall, interesting course with some good material. But could be far more organized on the administrative end.
Poor structure. Projects seemed random and felt like they had little planning. Late policy was an instant 0 which is unheard of for a project based course.

Homeworks are hard and can take quite some time to figure out a solution, but you have 2-3 weeks to do them. Exams were difficult as well, but it seems like there is a generous curve at the end of the course (75% got me a B). Regarding the lectures, they feel very useful as Childs will go through the material thoroughly and is good at checking for questions and answering them.

Dr BG was extremely knowledgeable and passionate about the material. His lectures were pretty hard to follow but he made it very easy to ask questions and gave alternative sources to learn materials. His homework’s were very fair and helped with my overall understanding of the course material. The exams were extremely difficult and the average was low but he curves accordingly. Overall I had a positive experience in Dr Boyd-Graber’s NLP class.

I feel like he relies way too much on his TA's for the class and doesn't really care for the class at all. You pretty much have to self-learn everything which is pretty hard if you don't have much experience with coding.

There’s one required discussion, optional lectures (in my opinion), and a semester-long project. Most of the work is asynchronous, so it’s pretty manageable. I actually liked the assignments, they’re straightforward and teach you exactly what you need to know. You don’t interact with the professors much (there are two), but Professor Duffy stands out as super understanding and clear about expectations. She’s chill, and overall I enjoyed the class.

Please DO NOT TAKE THIS CLASS WITH THIS MAN. He taught us nothing at all, did not explain anything and never showed up to his own office hours. He never reschedules the things he cancels, does not give you enough time to complete his vague assignments, and somehow expects you to get it. He does not publish any information and lectures until after we needed it, which it practically useless. The class discord what a wreck and he never gets around to anything. Please if you value your GPA, your time, and your sanity, don't bother with this class.

TAKE HIM. Does not prepare you that well for the final but your grade in the class will be so good (Mine was 95) that it does not matter. The midterms are EXACTLY LIKE THE PRACTICE TEST. You should get 100. My friend somehow got an A- in the class by getting a 93 on the final but that was insane because his grade was so low before. AND he curves. Its a no brainer take him for MATH140.
Good lecturer but is an awful grader, no curving exams or final grades. Low 70s averages with class average being in the 70s, with many kids stressing for the final to even pass the class (with a C).

Qi'An did a really good job! He gave us a good amount of practice problems during discussion, explained things clearly, and helped us understand the parts we needed to know for the exams. I had him for MATH240, and I was often confused during lecture or just bored because it wasn't clear what was relevant to class, but during discussion with him I knew he was always talking about things we needed to know. He also sent us solutions for practice exams which were very helpful.

Responded well to criticism and made changes in the middle of the semester to accommodate for his students. For example, the homework at the beginning of the semester was very hard compared to what he makes now. The homework is much more relevant to what we are doing in class, and he created bonus questions for those of us who want a bump to our grade. Another example is how he helped us prepare for midterm 2. Although he released the practice questions a little late, they were very helpful for what we would see on the test. I went from a <50% midterm 1 grade, to just barely a 90% on midterm 2. Also, he curved exams that had an average below 83 generously. To everyone reading all of his reviews and preparing for the worst, I promise you its not that bad at all. Some people are just coping such as the review below mines.
Easiest A of my life, but also the most frustratingly pointless class I have ever taken. Do not take Anurag Dey, especially for a course you want to use as a prerequisite for future courses.

I think this is one of the most fair reviews you will get as this was my first ever computer science course ever. The only reason he is not a 1 star is because he records lectures, is a nice person, and does the bare minimum for previous quizzes and practice exams. But when it comes to being an actual professor he is simply not good at all. I do not get why other people are giving high reviews if they think he is boring. Many students skip his lectures because he often just goes through some half baked slides and goes on tangents about something we never need to learn or a concept we learned weeks ago in class. When it comes to teaching concepts, he does almost everything poorly except for memory maps which aren't on any of our classes exams or finals but it was for other students. Also his exams 1 and 3 as well as quizzes 3 and 5 were completely different and way more difficult then his practice exams. ANOTHER big issue with Pedram was his timing. We learned all the material for exam 3 way before thanksgiving break but instead our exam was right after break. Many people including myself would have much rather spent time with our families instead of studying for a class in which other professors gave their students their 3rd exam before break. All the other classes had way more time to study for finals and I was even using other classes study material to learn concepts because what Pedram gives simply is not good enough. Lastly, discussions were pretty much useless unless it was a day before a quiz or exam. I would learn a concept from brocode 10x quicker then a discussion, and I do not get why our quizzes were not in there like the other CS Classes so we could actually learn content in class.

Mr. Herman (not professor, don't call him that he'll go on a tangent about addressing him incorrectly) is a pretty good professor. I think he gets a lot of hate because you aren't allowed to use any electronic devices during lecture, but he does it so you can actually focus in class. Some lectures can be quite boring if you kind of of already know what he's talking about, but I felt he covered the course material really well. His lecture slides contained a lot of the content that you needed to know for the class, so reviewing them before every exam was very helpful. He also provides example code that help you understand how concepts work if you are unable to understand it immediately. He does waste the beginning of class for reminders that no one really needs to hear. Exams were very fair. He gave practice material that reflected exactly what was on the exam. As long as you study hard for the exams, it should be pretty easy to get an A. No lecture recordings, and you have to attend lecture and discussion every time because he will randomly have graded worksheets. They are 11% of your grade but is a guaranteed 100 as long as you show up. 3% is class participation, so just raise your hand 3 times during the semester. Overall, a very solid professor. If he is the only option you have, there's nothing to worry about. You will still learn everything you need to know, just accustom yourself to how he runs the class.

If you want an easy grade without really learning anything, take Nelson. He tries to be funny, but that's not what I came to school for. I wish I had taken 216 with somebody who actually cares more about teaching than just being popular. I got an A, but I don't really feel prepared for upper level courses that might depend on 216.

He'll lure you in with a 40% homework grade (it's graded harshly), a 10% discussion grade(only free part of the course), and low weighted midterms and finals. The midterms were really bad, especially the first one. He never makes clear what's going on in the course. Nobody knew what the cutoffs for an A, A-, B+, ect were. Extra credit is almost worthless (0.05% per). He was extremely disorganized for all his lectures, he was late for 2 or maybe all 3 midterms so we lost valuable time (compensated with 0.5 extra credit points on a 32 point midterm). That being said. He's a chill guy and explained concepts in a really fun way. I liked his laid back approach focusing on more of the conceptual aspect as opposed to something more stingy on format (like Fawzi). If it weren't for the above issues he'd get 4 stars.

Take this class for the plot but not if you actually want to learn anything. I don't understand how Max had some level of success in the industry as he literally didn't understand that not all data that is bell curved shaped is a normal distribution(among many other obvious things). It was entertaining to watch him be confused and say the most out of pocket things("A human life is worth $2000. If I donate $2000 every year I can do whatever I want because I've already contributed positively") Homework's were time consuming but interesting and probably good practice. Exams were poorly written and poorly graded(got 5-10% on every exam via regrade request). They were hard not because they tested tough concepts or required an in depth knowledge to do well but just because they attempted to ask you a very specific thing vaguely but ended up doing it weirdly. Advice: do really well on the HWs. Extra credit is awarded for extra long reports, pretty reports and using concepts not discussed in class so make an effort to do these things on your report. Getting a 110% or higher on an assignment worth almost as much as an exam will allow you to do pretty poorly on the exams and still do well in the class. Also do the readings closely. He asks pretty specific questions on the exams.
Only complaint is that he tends to mumble sometimes, so I would recommend sitting near the front so you can hear everything he says. Solid lecturer. Makes the topics about as engaging as they can be.

It was a fine class. Content is not difficult but his exams can be tricky. The good thing is his exams are similar to practice (structure wise). I think some of the point distributions were unfair though. The big change I noticed from his other classes and this is the powerpoints are very bland. There wasn't really enough content on them to answer questions. So it forces you to watch the lectures or go to class (obviously most choose to watch lectures). That being said I think if you learn content from the practices and project you can set yourself up for at least a decent grade.

I found Ting's lectures very hard to follow. The slides presented information in a sort of confusing way, and her poor handwriting and strong accent made it a little hard for me to understand what was going on when we were getting into more difficult concepts. I ended up mostly using Justin's class notes and online resources because they were much easier to learn from. Since they co-teach, this worked out fine for homeworks and exams. If you, like me, are not a morning person, you are probably better off with Ting.

Please take this class with her because the way she teaches the content will make sense. The exams are based on practice questions, homeworks, and exercises demonstrated in the slides. Computer Arch is a lower level topic so it could be confusing, but her step by step explanations make it clear. She's very nice during office hours and is willing to help clear your confusion. The projects aren't bad as long as you start around a week before due date. Also, the professor and TA (Jerry Gui) answered piazza questions quite well and detailed, which also was a plus. Overall 11/10 class. STRONGLY RECOMMENDED.

I would give ZERO stars if I would. This is both the hardest and worst course that I've ever had the displeasure of taking at UMD. I enrolled in this class because I thought that Operating Systems is a fundamental and useful skill to learn, even if difficult, but found out that the administration of this class makes this 10x more harder for literally no reason. There are so many things wrong with this course that I wouldn't recommend ANYONE taking it because it's not worth it. First of all, others seemed to like the professor's lecturing ability, but I did not. He goes on tangents all the time and is very unclear in his statements that it is impossible to focus. The slides are comprehensive, but are taken straight from the textbook so that isn't really a credit to the professor. The projects and exams though, that is a different hell. Let's talk projects. Each one is incredibly difficult, and the instructions are HORRIBLE. There is really no valid reason why there should be a spec, slides, and FAQ for EVERY SINGLE PROJECT. The spec is awfully written and flat out wrong about things, the project slides are vague and also have incorrect information. The FAQs don't answer certain questions with any new information, and the fact that an FAQ is even needed for a project means that the instructions are poorly written. And to make things worse, even the spec, slides, and FAQ are sometimes not enough. On a related note, administration for this course was TRULY TERRIBLE. Questions on Piazza were just left unanswered even though there were many people with the same question; the TAs just didn't answer and weren't active. I'm pretty sure they were also left in the dark about logistics in the class, because it was near the end of the semester and we STILL did not have breakdowns of grading. That part of the course website was just never filled out. And one of our pop quizzes, which we only had 10 minutes to do and had a very poor average, was worth almost an entire project grade. That is completely ridiculous and shows how little the professor cares about administration for this class. For exams, we didn't get any review material, no study guide or previous exams, zip, zilch, nada. Just "look at the slides" which are hundreds if not thousands of slides so it's impossible to study everything on it. In addition, for our final, the professor was very unaccommodating to concerns over the Omicron variant, and refused to move the final online despite multiple CS classes shifting online, and almost the entire class requesting this change. No reasoning was given, of course. Lastly, our final exam, which is worth a quarter of our final grade, was put on the grade server, and we never even got it back to see what we got wrong, let alone a regrade request. It was simply put on Testudo. This fact may change since this review is posted, but nevertheless it is inexcusable to have these final grades submitted without students seeing the reason, especially when this resource is easily available via Gradescope. I get that Operating Systems is a hard concept, but like I said, the administration made this course needlessly more difficult. I am sure that most other people in the class agree with me regarding the majority of the points that I raised here, and there are probably more points that I didn't mention. These points are definitely fixable (having clear grading, clear project descriptions, enforcing Piazza answering, giving us study material) and should definitely be addressed the next time this course is taken. I find that unlikely to happen though, so I do not recommend this course to anyone until then. You're better off looking at the slides or textbook on your own.

Flipped classroom model yada yada yada. Judge yourself whether you will actually succeed in that type of environment. Marsh as a professor is knowledgeable and tries to do everything he can for his students. His slides are utterly useless in terms of actually learning what to do, so you will have to do most of the learning on your own (which really doesn't help in the flipped classroom model) or figure it out somehow, which leads me to the the biggest problem with this class: the projects. They are incredibly difficult, no two ways about it. Somehow I managed to complete them but oh boy was it stressful. I also am not really interested in the class content, so that definitely didn't help. Also, one thing to note is that this class HEAVILY leans into computer security rather than network security. Do not think this class's content will give you enough information comparable to 417.

Justin is a great lecturer who really makes the content engaging and easy to digest, and he posts great notes as well if you miss class. The seven exam structure was interesting, but I quite liked it. Given we had a midterm dropped and that the exams generally reflected the given practice material it was not too difficult to prepare for, and I found it less stressful to study one or two topics than studying a bunch of topics for two or three exams. Just start reviewing practice problems and making sure you understand how the exams DS works a couple of days before the exam and you should be good to go. The projects aren't too bad and have no secret test which is nice, and one is dropped. Great class, would recommend.

Mr Regli is a really nice guy and super helpful if you ever talk to him one on one. However, there were countless issues for this course. Projects with conflicting directions, instructions in 5 different places making it hard to know everything, TA "recitations" where they just read off a slide and couldn't answer basic questions, exams where students had to argue for points back due to unclear wording, etc. Easily the most disorganized class I've taken at UMD, making it hard to engage with the material and actually learn. His lectures are also completely all over the place and impossible to follow. By the third week no one was even attempting to take notes because he goes so fast and its not clear which information is relevant at all. For the final, the whole class really struggled because everyone studied the wrong material, myself included. He did curve the exam(s), so in his defense he made up for a lot of his mistakes. I also did get an A in the class, so it all worked out in the end to be fair. However, CMSC421 has been a terrible class at UMD for years.

I genuinely wanted to learn this material, but the way the course was run made that almost impossible. It’s hard to express how much I dislike this course. It’s structured very poorly: it’s extremely fast-paced with almost no room to actually retain the material. The assignments don’t reflect what you need to know to do well on the exams, and the textbooks are pretty unhelpful if you’re new to ML. I’m not even going to say much about the grading (yes, it’s very punitive, likely due mostly to the TAs) because others have already covered that. The instructor seems to assume that if one person gets an A on the midterm, then everyone should be able to get an A, which completely ignores the reality that students juggle many responsibilities. It’s not just “do research,” “teach,” eat, and sleep. Her teaching style ends up overwhelming students and reinforcing unnecessary competition, especially coming from someone who didn’t go through the same level of modern academic pressure, unstable economy, or constant distractions. Overall, the class was mentally draining because of the uncertainty around how to actually learn and retain the material, what to expect on exams, and how to find reliable resources for long-term understanding. By the second midterm, the stress had taken a significant toll on, I’m sure, the majority of the class. Amazing and thank you!

This was the most difficult class I've ever taken at UMD, and I do not know why it was necessary for it to be this way. The participation quizzes in lecture are grading on accuracy, the reading quizzes during the week are difficult, and the exams are absolutely brutal. Avoid this professor at all costs and take another semester to actually enjoy learning about databases instead of tearing your hair out.

DVH is alright. Good lectures with plenty of dry humor. Projects are hard outside of the first two but manageable so long as you get started early. Helpful TAs on Piazza (shoutout Pierce). Easy quizzes/surveys, and access to some excellent notes which can supplement lecture. My main problem is how disorganized things are, deadlines are set but rarely met, when he says something will be out Tuesday expect it to be on Thursday or even later. Also no late credit if you turn things in late. If you enjoy this class check out CMSC838E with DVH, the grad level version where you go even more in-depth into these very same topics.

Man. So you thought 433 was always just going to be Java multithreading right? NOPE! Turns out, it's just whatever the professor wants to teach. This guy, Mr. Rance Cleaveland, was all about programming correctly, because in theory, the more correct your code is, the more secure it is. Neat concept. Nice. Cool beans. Quite a shame, because he clearly can't run a class about it. His class is structured around a single paper mathy assignment, several projects in Dafny and Haskell (dafny is extremely cringe and haskell is just ocaml part 2), one midterm, and one final. Oh, you want to study for the midterm or the final? Yeah sure man, all you have to study is a single slide of a presentation showing all the topics you need to know. No example problems. No practice exam. No textbooks. I guess you have the singular homework that wasn't a project. At least the exam is open computer, closed internet, but doesn't really help when you have zilch to study from. For me, his lecture was quite boring and rather un-learn-able for someone who isn't interested in learning what ancient Mesopotamian symbol I need to know this time. The projects were either incredibly easy or extremely annoying and frustrating, either due to the language or the extremely poor project description. There were multiple Piazza questions all asking about what he meant by the projects and he basically answered them full of academic jargon that probably makes sense conceptually. So basically, his class has zero structure and you're supposed to already be a god and know this kinda stuff in order to do well. The class is not easy despite the workload being low. It just felt like he finally found a hundred people or so willing to listen to him talk about whatever he's been studying for the past however many years.

I'd give 4.7 stars if PlanetTerp had such an option. This is a hard class. Not in the way that MATH140/141 are considered "hard", or in the way that Kruskal's classes are "hard" (at least his 351), but rather it is hard by virtue of the material. Algorithms are just often difficult concepts to grasp and really understand to the depth that Childs' wants his students to be able to grasp and understand for his assignments and exams. The class is paced quite nicely for me - I showed up to every lecture, and I feel like I gained something from each one. I was able to ask questions pretty frequently (perhaps too frequently), and Childs' would always spend the time to think about an answer to each one, and I felt that that helped me understand the material greatly. He records all of his lectures and posts all of his notes. The only things from class not available asynchronously online are the Q&A times that he holds in the 5-10 minutes before each class begins. The assignments are hard. (Did I mention the class is hard?) The first two took me about 10 hours each, and the other three 15-20 hours each. Each one is a set of five problems, the answers to which require (unless you're a super-mega-genius I guess) intuition and material from the lectures. A quote from one of his office hours: "If you're stuck on this problem, think about the algorithms we covered in class; I make the homeworks directly related [to those]." - Childs My strategy for the homeworks were to look at the problems when they were assigned, then keep them in mind over the next two weeks of lectures (each assignment is assigned exactly two weeks before they're due). Spending the time to actually understand the material on them is definitely helpful - they're actually harder than the exam questions by a solid margin, and they mirror the exam structure. Also, he drops the lowest of the five assignments, so each of your best four assignments comprise 10% of your final grade. Considering that there is ample time for each one, it's definitely possible to have the assignments be the grade fallback. The exams are hard. (yes.) The midterm is worth 20% of your final grade, and the final 40%. There's definitely a time-crunch aspect to this. As of writing this review, I haven't taken the final yet. But speaking from the midterm experience, there wasn't a single student that left the exam room early (shocker). Although it seemed like most of the class felt pretty bad about the midterm, to Childs', the midterm was "on the easier side." (Avg 69, median 70 iirc) I did well enough not to have major complaints about it, and other reviews go more in-depth. The textbook is... something that I didn't read. I'm sure it was useful to those who did, but the lectures + questions + office hours + assignments prepared me well enough to face the exams. Although Childs' is a great lecturer and all-around smart guy, he's definitely a bit hard to talk to. He feels like a classic computer-focused guy (which is fair, since he's getting paid for it lol), and I definitely agree with the previous reviewer that said it felt impossible to build rapport with him. TL;DR: Great lecturer, fair class, hard af so look at the grade distr. to make your choice

She's a first time professor. In terms of lectures, she did try to make the content more understandable, and I think her explanations do, at times, make a significant improvement to the readings. While the difficulty and grading was not challenging as long as you listened to the lectures, the timing was a mess and it was never explained why it took so long for homework and midterms. Furthermore, the number of homework assignments were constantly changing throughout the course. I really hoped to learn more about NLP from this course. While the theoretical content was there, I am still not sure if there was enough technical support, with coding, to make this enriching to take as a course. As another review mentioned, there is a lot of room for improvement. But, there's only one way up if you're at the bottom.

Aric is a very nice person and tries to get to know all of his students and finds interest in them. I truly believe that I learned a lot from this class, but in the least efficient way possible. His class is a completely in-person class, but if I want to know the information and do well on the exams, I need to watch the lecture videos he assigns, which took me an average of 2 hours a week outside of class alone. He is one of the most disorganized professors I have had, and it becomes evident in very important situations. There's a group project at the end of the semester that is so rushed and is just an addition to continuing with everything else we have been doing the rest of the semester and the expectations of how much he wants us to include in it are unreasonable. If you take his class, which I think you could learn a lot from, be prepared to devote a lot of time to it outside of class and be forced to create your own organizational system for his class because he does a terrible job at doing that himself.

Horrendous teacher, don't get how she is 4.3 stars. I took her because I got a recommendation from a friend, as well as the good PlanetTerp reviews. She creates a GroupMe for the class, then accuses half the class for cheating because we asked questions in it? I stopped going to lecture but she tries to make jokes mid lecture and all of them are bricks. Although she knows the material and can somewhat teach, she's just miserable to have, just find a better professor (not hard). She needs to wrap it up at this point

If you want a professor who holds office hours, communicates with students, does things on time, or explains things, DO NOT TAKE INST414 with him. He would regularly cancel office hours and tell us he's rescheduling but never reschedule. He told us he'd hold an additional weekly review for us, but never held any. He would publish lecture videos and assignments at the last minute. He also promised us that he would have review videos before each assignment, but they were published after the assignments. The overall communication is just poor. He is slow to respond in the class Discord and via email.
My grade got better after I stopped showing up to her lectures and read the textbook on my own. I think that speaks for itself.

Dr. Ebrahimian is a very professional guy and a talented lecturer. He will aptly answer any question to make sure everything is understood. Math 141 is a difficult course, however, and it's important to stay on top of topics by doing as much practice as you can (assigned homework problems and worksheets).

Wiseley Wong is the goat. Although he is a chalkboard lecturer, his handwriting is very clear and he only writes on the middle ones so everyone can see. He explains concepts very well and always tells you what will be on the quizzes. 15% for 3 exams, 30% final, 15% quizzes, and 10% matlab. Everything was very fair, the true/false questions are a pain but they prepare you for the final! He answers questiosn very well and is not afraid to call people out for talking really loud in his lectures! And no curve because his exam scores are so high, midterm averages are around 80%.

Not as bad as the other reviews say at all, was a little bit rough at first but he improved as a lecturer throughout the course. Also listened to student feedback, helped us prepare better for midterm 2, eventually curved Midterms 1 and 2, and added bonus points on homework. Nice guy, sometimes a little confusing examples but provided more relevant and easy to understand examples. His first time teaching and he definitely got better throughout, 1 star rating is 100% undeserved. Also does have fire fits every class.

A goated professor who cares about students success and is very helpful. He is very lenient with grading and has fair exams but be sure to study as things could get tricky. PROS: 1) Good grading 2) Nice professor 3) Small class CONS: 1) Not recored lecture 2) Somewhat theoretical at some points I call him MDDKG and he is one mountain goat

Highkey a bum professor, his lectures are recorded but are very boring. This year he decided to change the curriculum, meaning that all his previous exams/quizzes were useless. This gave Pedram the chance to make them annoyingly hard, no matter how much you studied. If you know the material beforehand then you are fine, but if not then you might be in some trouble. This is known as one of the weed out classes, however no need for him to make his exams so much harder than what he did previous years.

CS instructor (not professor, as he made very clear), yet no electronics are allowed any time in class. Not afraid to single people out if you leave lecture early. Assigned an exam immediately after fall break and immediately after thanksgiving break, so be prepared to study during all your breaks! Projects aren't so bad, but exams are pretty hard. Optional homework (but you should probably do them they actually are helpful). Graded on participation which is kind of weird for a lecture of 200+ people. All of his lecture slides are posted on Canvas as files so you have to individually download each one to view them, same goes for homework and projects, which was kind of annoying. Herman also doesn't answer his email and specifically asks you not to email him so the only opportunity you'll have to ask questions is office hours. Overall it isn't terrible, but I'd say try for a different professor if you can.

One of the best professors I have ever had. I think he truly structures his course through a student's perspective. The fact that he records his lectures and lab walkthroughs really allowed me to fully understand the course concepts. I feel like he gave adequate practice materials for exams and although they were REALLY long, his projects were one of the biggest reasons I did well in this course. His long and intensive projects covered basically everything that we would need to know for the course and doing the projects helped me not only understand the topics conceptually but also in practice. My advice to future students would be to really understand the projects because thats usually what the coding question for exams will be based off of.

Fawzi was absolutely fantastic! He definitely expects students to come to the lectures, and it was so worth it! (Isn't that what we're paying for?) The lectures were fun and he made everything super easy to understand. Fawzi really cares about his students and does everything he can to make sure that they are really learning and not just going through the motions. He's preparing us for harder courses later (like 351). The solutions to the homework questions were always posted online, and we had plenty of materials to study (homework, worksheets from the discussion classes, and the lecture examples). He also gave out very high grades! Fawzi was amazing and I highly recommend him for any class he teaches!

Max is probably the most interesting lecturer that I’ve had within the CS department at UMD. As somebody with a chronic class-skipping problem, I found myself only missing one or two of his lectures. His exams are tougher than most, but the grade distribution balances out such that his class is very passable without doing well on them, and the vision behind his questions is one I can understand, as he is actively trying to teach his students applicable material to a professional job and not just formulaslop.

Anwar is nice, but I really hate his style of teaching since it’s so disengaging. Literally on the first day of class, bro just opened up Emacs and started coding random stuff, and he doesn’t reference his slides at all—or barely does. It’s so hard to take notes or follow along with what he’s saying when he just codes for 1 hour and 15 minutes straight. Towards the end of February, I started skipping lecture since he unnecessarily went way too in-depth into the concepts and didn’t teach them in the way they actually show up on the quizzes and exams. This class is nice though because the projects make up a big portion of your grade, and the exams aren’t worth that much. I literally failed the first two exams and did well on the final, and I’m ending with an A- (that’s telling you how easy it is to do well in this class if you lock in on projects). Quizzes are each only 2% of your grade, but they add up so try to do well on them. You just need to study 2–3 days in advance and do the practice, and you’ll be fine. The TAs are way more involved in this course compared to other CS classes, but some of them clearly don’t know anything about the concepts. Also, some are super unhelpful on Piazza, not directly answering questions but posting a link to something else because they're too lazy to answer LMAO. But luckily my discussion TA was super smart, so he was very helpful. Overall, this class won’t be too bad, but try to study in advance and get ahead if you can to make it easier on yourself.

This professor is insanely disorganized and very very very bad at teaching. He uses Nelson's material, which is fine but the issue is that he does not prepare at all. It felt like he did not know any web-dev. He is very unprepared during lectures and just reads what's written in the slides. When a student is paying nearly $5000 for one course, the least he can do is read the material before presenting it. DO NOT TAKE CMSC-335 with him.

Terrible professor. He doesn't care about the class at all; he always came to class late, he never graded in a timely manner, when he released solutions to homework and practice exams they were almost always incomplete, and more than a few times outright incorrect. When answering questions, both in person and online, his answers are typically vague and unhelpful (he is also hard of hearing, so it will take some effort and some help from the people in the front row to get his attention). Going to his class is useless most of the time, just go do the homework instead. His lectures didn't contain testable material until the last few weeks, and he always fumbled through them, as though he only half remembered the material. I think it's likely that he made his slides years ago and only looks at them during class when he has to deliver them. All the material that appeared on homework and exams (until like three weeks from the end) was given through video lectures. There were two kinds of these. The first was videos he recorded at home during the pandemic, and these are actually quite good. It's very useful to see his process when trying to replicate it on the homework. The second type was recordings taken of him delivering the lecture in a normal class, and these are much worse. The sound quality is terrible, there's a ton of awkward silences, he spends a lot of time answering questions from students who you can't hear, and they take about twice as long as the first type to cover the same amount of material. The homework is hard, but not as hard as understanding what it wants you to do in the first place. Logistically the entire class was a nightmare. He didn't give us a syllabus until the second week of classes. He made his midterms two hours long, which required booking different rooms to hold them in, which took him a ton of time to make work, which meant that we didn't learn the actual dates of the midterms until the week before. By the end of the semester he was well over a month behind on grades. Final grades were due on Friday, May 23rd, and we got them on Tuesday, May 27th. The exams are heavily based on the homework, usually copypasting the hardest problem from a recent homework and changing the numbers. Reminder again that they are two hours long. Just leaving this here: https://www.cs.umd.edu/classconcern Avoid at all costs.

I am shocked to see so many people up in arms about the high number of midterms in this class. It seems like I am in the minority when I say I didn't mind this structure and actually kind of liked it. Justin changed his CMSC420 course structure this semester to be very largely exam-based, with a "midterm" exam every two weeks. He did this with the idea that if he assigned homework, students would just ChatGPT the whole thing (and he's probably not wrong). At surface level, this does sound atrocious and I was worried at first. But there is a pro to this structure: there were no major midterm exams that required cramming a huge amount of content into your brain, like most classes. Each exam was entirely focused on the material we had covered since the last exam, which was at max two weeks, or five lectures, of material. Thus, there was only so much he could possibly test on, making studying easier (for me at least). The rest of the things that people have praised Justin for over the years haven't gone away: his super engaging lectures, his detailed and organized notes, and his stellar focus on helping students succeed. For every topic we covered, he had a set of organized optional problems on that topic available on ELMS. Before each exam, he would post on Piazza which questions within those problem sets to focus on when studying. So my studying usually consisted entirely of working through those suggested problems, which was enough to get me As on just about every exam. Maybe the material just clicked with me in a way that it didn't for others, but I had to study for like maximum two hours for each exam. As such, I actually liked this structure because for me, it kept the workload outside of class pretty light. Study for an exam one night every two weeks, do the occasional project here and there (these were pretty straightforward, enjoyable, and well-explained). He also drops the lowest exam grade and lowest project grade, so there's a nice cushion for error there too. I'm not sure if he will keep doing this in the future, because he has seen the negative feedback here and elsewhere and has acknowledged that he wasn't aware some students would have such major stress in regards to this class. TL;DR: If you are a student who tends to study a LOT for exams and tends to get really stressed before exams, I would stay away from this class with Justin, because you'll probably fall into the same hole as a lot of these 1-star reviewers. But if you're someone like me who doesn't stress too much over exams, I imagine this class will feel light for you too. Justin is still a top-notch lecturer and professor, and I loved learning this content from him.
